title: Three times
hookLine: Peter denied Jesus three times; after the resurrection he is asked three times, lovest thou me? (John 21:15–17)

cards: I am not. Three short words, said in a courtyard at night, and it's cold. Servants and officers have made a fire of coals and stand around it warming their hands.
Peter is standing with them. Inside, Jesus has been arrested and is being questioned. A girl at the door asks Peter if he's one of this man's disciples.
He says no. Then someone else asks. Then someone else.
Three times, he says no. And then the rooster crows.

teach.b: First, the failure. Peter is the one who said he would lay down his life for Jesus. And when it counted, he warmed his hands by someone else's fire and said he didn't know him.
Luke adds a detail that's hard to read: "the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." And then: "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Just a look, and a grown man crying outside.
Second, the second fire. At the end of John's Gospel, after the resurrection, some of the disciples have gone back to fishing.
They come in at dawn and find Jesus on the shore, and John says: "they saw a fire of coals there." The same picture as the courtyard, with breakfast cooking on it. Third, the three questions.
After they eat, Jesus turns to Peter: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?" Peter says: "Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee." Jesus says, "Feed my lambs."
Then he asks again, and a third time, and John says Peter was grieved because he was asked the third time. Three denials, three questions. Every no in the courtyard gets a yes by the fire.

teach.h: FEED MY SHEEP: A REAL TASK.
teach.b: Each answer comes with work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep.

teach.h: THOU KNOWEST THAT I LOVE THEE.
teach.b: Not probation. Not a lecture. Jesus doesn't mention the denial at all.
He gives the man who failed the care of the others. Some Christians call this the restoring of Peter: the second chance comes with a real task, handed over by the fire.

how: In Christian teaching, John 21 is read as the restoring of Peter after his denial, and some preachers draw attention to the two fires of coals that frame the story.

o: the nights Peter spent hiding in fear after the arrest
Peter's three denials, then three yeses by a fire
the three days before the tomb was found empty

p: feed my lambs, feed my sheep

s: Jesus brings up the denial and makes Peter apologize
he never mentions it; he asks lovest thou me, and gives Peter work.
John uses the same picture, a fire of coals, in both scenes
a fire of coals in the courtyard, and a fire of coals on the shore.
Peter was grieved when he was asked the third time
John says so directly: he was grieved because he said unto him the third time.

games.q: you're Peter, eating breakfast on the shore with the one you denied three times. what does Jesus say to you?
o: he reminds you of the courtyard.
he tells you to go home.
games.why: he asks three times, "lovest thou me?" and each yes is answered with a job: feed my lambs, feed my sheep.

practice: Think of someone who let you down and has been trying, clumsily, to come back, a friend who flaked, a sibling who said the wrong thing, and picture them by a small fire, asking if things can be all right.
Notice whether you've kept them at the door, and imagine giving them one real chance, a small task, a bit of trust; if the one who failed is you, picture being asked the question and answering yes.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Three times. Peter's three denials in the courtyard, and his three answers by a fire on the shore: thou knowest that I love thee. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a second chance. Three denials, three yeses by the fire. Day nine hundred fifty-three.
